title: Bidirectional BFS in Mumbai: Double-Speed Paths!
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS race from both start and target on real street-map style graphs, meeting in the middle. This visualization highlights how expanding two frontiers drastically reduces search space and time.
ig_caption:
🚦 Mumbai (Worli) street-grid vibes—now with ⚡ Bidirectional BFS ⚡

In graph theory terms, Bidirectional BFS runs two simultaneous BFS searches: one from the **start node** and one from the **goal node**, expanding level-by-level. Because BFS explores shortest-path layers, the first time the two frontiers **intersect**, you’ve effectively stitched together the optimal shortest route with far fewer visited nodes than classic single-source BFS.

🗺️ Think of intersections as vertices and street connections as edges (unweighted like “one move = one hop”). On a real-world street-map graph, this “meet-in-the-middle” strategy can turn a sprawling search into a focused collision point—especially helpful when the start and target are far apart.

fb_caption:
In today’s video, we visualize **Bidirectional BFS** on a street-map style graph from Mumbai (Worli)! 🌍

Graph search finds paths by treating intersections as nodes and streets as edges—Bidirectional BFS improves efficiency by running BFS from both the start and the goal until the frontiers meet, reducing unnecessary exploration.
